Edition note: An independent English rewriting for English-language readers, preserving the Chinese argument while reorganizing context, sequence, and emphasis. Full-series spoilers.

The list

Charlotte York has a list, and she does not apologize for it. A husband, but not just any husband: well brought up, tall, presentable, professionally established, from a suitable family. A church wedding, a white dress, bridesmaids, vows. An apartment with a doorman, preferably on Park Avenue. Two children. A dog.

The list attracts jokes from Samantha and Miranda, observations from Carrie, and an audience inclined to see Charlotte as the least modern member of the group. She can look like someone awaiting enlightenment. Before accepting that account, it is worth recognizing that the desire is hers. She wants a home, stability, someone to spend her life with, and the feeling of being wholeheartedly wanted.

Those wishes are neither shameful nor necessarily symptoms of false consciousness. Her world has supplied their familiar forms, but familiarity does not make her longing unreal. The series' more interesting undertaking is not to tear up the list and teach her not to want a family. It lets her obtain much of what is listed, then discover that the items do not necessarily contain what she wanted.

Trey

Trey MacDougal appears to answer the specifications. He comes from an established Scottish family, is a handsome, tall heart surgeon, and has the Park Avenue apartment. His mother Bunny knows exactly how things should be done, including the wedding. Charlotte and Trey become engaged quickly; the wedding is beautiful.

The night before it, Charlotte discovers his sexual difficulty. It is not simply an isolated awkward moment that marriage resolves. She marries him anyway. What follows is not most usefully understood as a story about a villain. Trey can be polite, gentle, and distressed by their difficulties. He makes efforts. Cruelty is not the only way a marriage can fail to provide a shared life.

Bunny occupies too much of the space between them. Charlotte often seems to have to pass through his mother before she can reach her husband. It would nevertheless be unfair to say he never stands up for her: during the divorce, his telegram tells Bunny to give Charlotte the apartment. That act of support matters. The problem is that local gestures of goodwill have not sustained the everyday companionship Charlotte needs.

She consults doctors, tries solutions, tries silence, moves out, and returns. Then she turns toward the next item on the list: a child. The painful possibility is that she is asking the next approved achievement to repair the previous one. Their attempts to conceive narrow her life into temperatures, cycles, and treatment. She can become sharp, obsessive, and difficult to be around. The longing does not become less real because it brings out unattractive behavior.

Charlotte also considers adoption and puts them on a waiting list for a Chinese child. Yet they have not arrived at a shared understanding of what they want. The marriage ends. Another checked box could not supply the relationship missing beneath the boxes.

What the list was holding

The central distinction is now available. The list was not the ultimate desire; it was the container Charlotte could imagine for that desire. In smaller, less photogenic terms, she wanted someone to eat breakfast with, someone present during illness, someone actually listening when she spoke. She wanted a place where maintaining an image was unnecessary, and a lifelong promise sincerely made.

These things did not become stable in her marriage. Trey could supply the prestigious family, profession, appearance, apartment, ceremony, and surname without those advantages generating the ordinary intimacy she wanted. A package can look complete while leaving its intended contents missing.

This is not proof that commitment or domestic life was the wrong wish. It is evidence that the familiar indicators were unreliable. The series takes apart Charlotte's container before it asks her to abandon her desire. That distinction matters: otherwise every failure of a conventional marriage becomes an easy argument that wanting marriage was foolish from the start.

Harry

Harry Goldenblatt, her divorce lawyer, scarcely resembles the man imagined by the list. He is bald, not tall, hairy, noisy at meals, and unconcerned with Charlotte's standards of presentation. He is Jewish, while she comes from an Episcopal background with a firm sense of its own identity. Their sexual relationship begins when she is low, and her initial response is to keep it separate from the respectable public account of her life.

Her later conversion cannot be explained adequately as either pure sacrifice or effortless self-discovery. Harry has promised his late mother that he will marry a Jewish woman. Charlotte studies, attends classes, and repeatedly approaches a rabbi. She does real work. A decision beginning in love can acquire meaning beyond the person who first occasioned it.

But sincerity does not prevent her from turning effort into an invoice. After converting, she prepares a Sabbath dinner while Harry remains distracted by a game. Her frustration grows until she brings their difference in attractiveness into the argument and demands a wedding date. She has done all this; why has he not delivered the answer?

Harry is hurt and leaves. Being chosen by Charlotte does not oblige him to occupy the position of a grateful inferior. His boundary is the turning point. She cannot immediately chase after him and restore everything. She has to live through his absence and eventually recognize that she misses him, not simply a ring proving her investment worthwhile.

Nor does she immediately discard her religious choice when they separate. Her commitment was real; so was the impulse to use it as leverage. Both truths have to remain visible. The new life she has chosen cannot become a debt another person must instantly repay.

Their eventual Jewish wedding is full of mishaps, far less immaculate than the first. Wedding and commitment have not vanished. They no longer have to appear in the one shape the old list authorized. Her happiness does not depend on the ceremony meeting its previous specifications.

Lily

The wish for children is the last and most thorough test. Charlotte and Harry pursue treatment, and a pregnancy ends in miscarriage. At moments, the old constriction returns: a whole life can again appear to consist of charts and medical attempts. The difference is not that disappointment has stopped hurting.

Harry already knows that she may be unable to conceive, and he has spoken of adoption. She does not first have to prove she can provide a child in order to deserve his love. There is room between “we want a child” and “you must give me a child.” That space changes the meaning of their efforts.

Adoption itself entails paperwork, scrutiny, waiting, disappointment, and more waiting. At the series' end, they receive a photograph of a Chinese girl. They will still have to wait six months before bringing her home. Charlotte nevertheless recognizes her as their child. The list's “two children” had carried an unstated picture of children she would bear. Lily comes from across the Pacific, without a biological connection, and belongs to the life Charlotte actually wanted.

Her unexpected pregnancy in the first film need not be read as a prize for patience or as compensation that finally makes the family complete. She is frightened throughout it because she knows what can be lost. It is another event in an already meaningful life, not a retroactive validation of the old checklist.

Charlotte has not relinquished family, commitment, or children. She has learned to distinguish them from the packaging she once trusted. Changing containers can be harder than abandoning the wish, because it first requires knowing which is which. Harry and Lily do not finish the old list. They help her recognize the life beneath it.

Sex and the City, created by Darren Star, aired from 1998 to 2004 across six seasons and ninety-four episodes, followed by films in 2008 and 2010.
